algorithm: Add learned gist tokens (Ng in {1,2,4,8}) after every sentence-ending punctuation mark. Gist tokens see their own sentence plus earlier gist tokens; regular tokens see their sentence plus gist tokens. Standard LM loss. Three stages: gist embeddings only, full fine-tune, large-batch cooldown. About 4B FineWeb-Edu tokens.
methodology: Llama-3.2-3B. Short context via lighteval; long context via HELMET-Tiny (4K-8K tokens). Baselines SepCache and Activation Beacon.
key_numbers: Ng=4: about 6x average long-context compression vs about 2x for Activation Beacon
Ng=4 HELMET recall 96 vs base 100; icl 63.2 vs 68.2
Ng=1: recall drops to 1.0, ARC 49.77 vs 59.21
limits: Rule-based placement, fixed budget per segment, punctuation sensitivity, does not fully recover base, full mask memory-heavy at 128K, only 3B tested.
use_for_project: Row [17] context compression, but needs fine-tuning and model access; not usable on hosted APIs.
corrections: 'No significant degradation' overstated: Ng=1 collapses recall and ARC; Ng=4 loses 4 to 5 points on recall and icl. 2x-8x is a KV-cache figure depending on Ng.

algorithm: CoThink: an instruct model (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) writes a 2-4 step outline with no numbers; the thinking model then expands it using only those steps. Defines token efficiency tau=Q/C and relative reasoning efficiency eta=(CR/CI)^beta, beta 0.3-0.5.
methodology: Four thinking models (DAPO, DeepSeek-R1-Distill, QwQ, Qwen3) on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24. Baselines Solo-Think, No-Think, Best-of-N (N=5, shortest).
key_numbers: Tokens cut 21.1% on average vs Solo-Thinking, up to 41.8%
Accuracy +1.66% on average
limits: Weak on GSM8K (DAPO +6.3% tokens, Qwen3 no-think +25.7%); math only; DAPO follows outline inconsistently; scaling law speculative; needs two models.
use_for_project: Row [45] overthinking / reasoning-token waste; a cheap-model outline prefix to bound thinking tokens.
corrections: 21.1% is an average, not uniform; some cells raise tokens or drop accuracy (Qwen3 think AIME24 -8.4%, R1-Distill AIME -19.0%). Win rate only 61.7%.

algorithm: GPT-4o-mini builds an answer-hint prefix in next-token form. Context split into m-token chunks; per chunk one focal token is generated ('none' drops the chunk). Attention to the focal token is summed over layers; top-k tokens select the sentences kept. Training-free, batched.
methodology: LongBench (2WikiMQA, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, GovReport) and BABILong. Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B readers; 8B/70B compressors. Baselines LLMLingua2, LongLLMLingua, BGE-M3 RAG.
key_numbers: Llama 2WikiMQA: 6.3x (small) and 15x (large) compression, EM 0.42 vs 0.49 original
HotpotQA latency 3.99s + 4.94s vs 19.36s original
Compression only 1.7x-2.0x on TriviaQA
limits: Needs attention access; attention aggregated over all layers; no explicit compression-ratio control; low ratio on TriviaQA.
use_for_project: Row [37] retrieved-context pruning; only with open-weight reader or local compressor, not hosted-model attention.
corrections: 'Up to 6.3x' understates the large setting (15x) and overstates typical (1.7x-4x). '~10% better than LLMLingua' is approximate. EM still below original.

algorithm: Self-MoA samples N outputs from the single best model (temperature 0.7); one aggregator synthesises them. Self-MoA-Seq aggregates with a sliding window of 6 responses. Regression of mixture performance on quality and Vendi-score diversity.
methodology: AlpacaEval 2.0 (six models), MMLU-redux, CRUX, MATH; over 200 experiments, over 70 mixtures for regression.
key_numbers: AlpacaEval LC: Self-MoA 65.7 vs Mixed-MoA 59.1 (+6.6)
Quality coefficient exceeds diversity coefficient (MMLU 2.558 vs 1.841)
Self-MoA with TaskBest averages +3.8%
limits: Mixed-MoA wins when models are similar in quality and complementary; gains not monotonic in samples; aggregator context limit.
use_for_project: Row [12] model mixing: a quality technique that multiplies calls (6 samples plus 1 aggregator); not a cost saver.
corrections: 3.8% is the TaskBest average. Cost rises per query; the earlier record is correct.

algorithm: Adapter protocol (create_agent, send_task, backup_session, delete_agent, get_docker_args); patch exported from git diff; history after base_commit removed to stop leakage. Lite-80 subset picked by quartile-quota local search with ranking hinge and cost-parity filter.
methodology: 350 instances, 43 repos, 8 languages; 7 harnesses x 3 models, 3 runs each (22,050 executions); max_turns 300, 3,600s timeout.
key_numbers: Bare adapter 19.3% vs full adapter 71.2% resolved; largest harness gap at fixed model 24.3 pp
Best Pass@1 Hermes Agent 81.7% at $36
Lite-80 vs full: MAE 0.81 pp at 25.3% of cost
limits: Meta-Harness evolved and evaluated on same instances; Lite is a proxy; appendix F is single-run.
use_for_project: Rows [5],[12]: harness choice moves outcome and cost at a fixed model; cache hit rates about 65%-97%.
corrections: Opus 4.7 vs DeepSeek-V4 Pro figures ($1,082.0 vs $81.3, 0.9 pp apart; about 13x) come from the one-run OpenClaw appendix, not the 3-run main table.

algorithm: Place the corpus as a directory of txt files (one JSONL for NQ) and give an off-the-shelf coding agent (Codex GPT-5; Claude Code Sonnet 4.5) only the path and query. It uses grep/rg, sed, nl and Python scripts iteratively. Configs: no retriever, BM25, Gemini embeddings.
methodology: BrowseComp-Plus, Oolong-Synthetic, Oolong-Real, LongBench-v2, NQ; 200-example samples; GPT-5 judge. Baselines full context, RAG, ReAct, RLM.
key_numbers: Beats published SOTA by 17.3% on average; SOTA on 4 of 5 benchmarks
Native search commands per trajectory 14.92 (no retriever) vs 8.33 (Gemini retriever)
GPT-5 full-context cost $1.421 per query on Oolong-Syn vs $0.275 on BrowseComp-Plus
limits: Retrievers did not consistently help; optimised for coding not long context; costlier than RAG; 200-sample evals; about equal to full context on LongBench.
use_for_project: Rows on context bloat and retrieval [30],[34]: filesystem plus grep slicing instead of stuffing context; cost vs quality trade-off.
corrections: Earlier record says cost not evaluated; the paper does report cost per query. 17.3% is an abstract-level average.

algorithm: Pairwise router (premium vs cheap). Bias between preference-based (PB) and gold-standard (GS) labels is a CATE, estimated with R- or DR-learners; pseudo-GS labels y+bias train a regressor on GS plus corrected PB. Route to premium if predicted gain exceeds cost factor w. GS scale normalised to PB scale.
methodology: HealthBench (5,000 dialogues), Gemini 2.5 Pro vs Gemma 3 12B, GPT-5-mini judge; n in {100,500,1000}; 200 Monte Carlo rounds. PRBench (676 questions).
key_numbers: PB-GS difference mean significantly below 0 (p<2.2e-16)
Meta-routers gain most when GS data is scarce
PRBench: DR-learner best at small n
limits: GS labels from an LLM judge not experts; pairwise only; needs overlapping query support; no headline cost number in text.
use_for_project: Row [12] routing: train a router from few verified labels plus many LLM-judge labels.
corrections: none (earlier record correctly notes no headline number)

algorithm: Roofline-style token latency: network/kernel time plus max(bytes, FLOP) terms; optimal batch b*=p*C/(B*2FLOP); NCCL all-reduce latency; MoE, KV and MLA reads; maximise (tokens/s)^alpha per price; speculative decoding expected tokens (1-a^g)/(1-a).
methodology: Pareto frontiers on H100 at $2/hr, checked against Artificial Analysis and PaLM data.
key_numbers: Latency scales with sqrt(params); each halving of weight precision cuts latency about 20%
Llama 3 70B at 4/8/16-bit: $0.23/$0.37/$0.70 per M tokens
Input tokens about 3x cheaper than output; Mistral Large 2 at 100K context about $6.06/M output (lower bound)
limits: Theoretical, H100-focused, assumed fixed context and independent expert routing.
use_for_project: Provider cost structure: why output and long-context tokens cost more; informs pricing model, not a client technique.
corrections: none; note text says alpha about 3 while Table 3 caption says 4.

algorithm: Per tier sample N=16 at T=0.7; nonconformity s=1-freq(a); split-conformal threshold from calibration; accept if prediction set size is between 1 and kappa, else defer to next tier. Cost c1+c2*Pr[|C1|!=1]; beats always-strong if Pr[|C1|=1]>c1/c2.
methodology: 18 multiple-choice benchmarks, four open families, 72 pairs, K=2, c1=1, c2=2.7, 30/70 calibration/test split.
key_numbers: Wins 49 of 72 pairs, ties 6, loses 17 vs oracle-tuned best heuristic
Llama/MMLU kappa 1 to 3 at alpha 0.10: cost 2.86 to 1.34 (-53%) at 5.3 pp accuracy cost
Tier-1 acceptance 0% (MMLU-Pro, GPQA) to 95.6% (Belebele-Eng)
limits: Finite answer sets only; marginal guarantee; K=2 only; needs 16 samples per tier and at least 200 labelled calibration examples.
use_for_project: Row [12] cheap-first cascade and escalation rule; sampling overhead is a cost caveat.
corrections: Guarantee is 1-K*alpha worst case (1-alpha only under selection preservation). Sampling cost is not free. 'Beats heuristics' holds on 49 of 72 pairs at oracle-tuned points.

read: full body (experiments read; appendix tables skipped)
algorithm: Train linear predictors guessing each layer's keys from the previous layer's keys, and values from previous-layer values plus current keys; quantize only the residual (Quanto or HIGGS backbone). Calibrate layer by layer on reconstructed inputs; keep first 4 tokens and a 128-token recent buffer in 16-bit.
methodology: Calibration on 256 RedPajama sequences of 8192 tokens; WikiText-2 perplexity and LongBench (14 tasks); Llama 3.x and Qwen 2.5 3B-72B. Baselines KIVI, KVQuant, KVSharer, HIGGS.
key_numbers: Near-lossless at 2-2.5 bits per value (under 1% relative error on Llama 3.2)
Calibration 4 hours on one GPU, at most 16GB VRAM, for Llama-3.1-70B
Predictor compute at least 500x below base model per token (70B/72B)
limits: Needs cache access and kernel support; unoptimized PyTorch about 3% slower than plain HIGGS; per-model calibration; 2-bit baselines degrade sharply.
use_for_project: none: provider or self-host KV memory technique; at most a long-context cost note.
corrections: none
new_techniques: inter-layer K/V linear predictors with residual quantization

algorithm: Longitudinal case study: Langfuse and vLLM telemetry plus Git mining. Fix Commit Ratio via regex over commit messages; difficulty-stratified Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio; TCO = M x (compute + ops + T_iter x wage); hybrid-routing offline counterfactual replay by difficulty tier.
methodology: Single developer, two 28-day periods: Claude Code with Opus 4.7/4.8 vs Opencode with GLM-5.1/5.2 NVFP4 on a shared Blackwell tray.
key_numbers: 99.3% cache hit cut API cost 88.6% to $0.57/M tokens vs $2.83/M shared on-prem
FCR 74.9% vs 45.9%; Mantel-Haenszel OR 3.61
Shared on-prem saves 40.1% true TCO; dedicated costs 43.8% more; High-to-Claude hybrid saves 26.3%
limits: One developer, non-randomized, tasks differ between periods; keyword-classified fixes; Period A fix count inflated by CI work; replay assumes tier exchangeability.
use_for_project: Rows [12],[2],[21],[50]: cache hit economics, cloud vs local TCO, hybrid routing frontier. Cached API can beat local per token.
corrections: none (earlier record accurate); add: no routing policy that sends any tier local matches pure-API defect rate.

algorithm: DeepSeekMoE: split each expert into m smaller ones and activate mK (fine-grained), plus Ks always-on shared experts; expert-level and device-level balance losses.
methodology: Validation at 2B on 100B tokens vs Hash Layer, Switch, GShard; 16B trained on 2T tokens vs DeepSeek 7B and LLaMA2 7B; SFT chat model; 145B preliminary.
key_numbers: DeepSeekMoE 16B matches LLaMA2 7B with 39.6% of computation
2B model matches GShard 2.9B (1.5x expert parameters and compute)
145B comparable to DeepSeek 67B with 28.5% of computation
limits: Weaker on multiple-choice tasks (limited attention parameters); 145B is preliminary.
use_for_project: none: model architecture; explains why MoE models are cheaper to serve per token.
corrections: Earlier record says 'matches LLaMA2 7B at about 40% compute': correct. 145B figure is 28.5% (maybe 18.2%).

algorithm: Multi-head Latent Attention caches a compressed latent c_KV (d_c=512) plus a decoupled RoPE key, so cache per token is (d_c+d_hR)*layers, equal to GQA with 2.25 groups. DeepSeekMoE FFNs, device-limited routing (at most 3 devices), YaRN extension to 128K, GRPO RL.
methodology: 236B total / 21B active, 8.1T tokens; H800 cluster; compared with DeepSeek 67B on training cost and throughput.
key_numbers: KV cache reduced 93.3% vs DeepSeek 67B
Generation throughput 5.76x; over 50K tokens/s on one 8-GPU node
Training cost down 42.5%; KV cache quantised to about 6 bits in deployment
limits: Shares usual LLM limits such as hallucination; mostly Chinese and English data.
use_for_project: none: provider-side architecture; explains cheap long-context pricing for MLA models.
corrections: none (earlier record accurate); throughput figure also uses FP8 weights and 6-bit KV quantization, not MLA alone.

read: Full text of p.txt (2229 lines), all of it: abstract, sections 1-8, references, Appendix A (Python sketch), B (proofs of Lemmas 2-7 and Theorems 1-2), C (greedy block verification, Lemmas 8-10, Theorem 3), D (Tables 5-10). Proofs followed at skim level, not re-derived.
algorithm: Block Verification replaces token-by-token rejection in speculative decoding. It computes p_i = min(p_{i-1}*Mb/Ms, 1) along the draft, accepts each sub-block with probability h_i (Eq. 5), keeps the longest accepted one, and samples the correction from a residual using p_i (Eq. 4). Same inputs, no extra model calls.
methodology: PaLM-2-S target with PaLM-2-XXS or XXXS draft, 8 datasets, first 1000 prompts, 128 output tokens, temperature 1.0, batch 1, 3 seeds. Spec-Bench with Vicuna-7B target and Vicuna-68M draft on one H100. Compared against token verification, greedy block verification, SpecTr and SpecInfer at batch 8.
key_numbers: XXS draft, gamma=8: block efficiency +8.30% avg (3.41 to 3.70, range 7.00-10.06%); wall clock +6.49% avg (2.30x to 2.45x, range 5.36-8.14%). XXXS gamma=8: +6.27% BE, +5.36% wall clock. Vicuna: up to +8.70% BE, +6.07% wall clock at T=1.0; +3.72% BE, +1.66% wall clock at T=0.2. Batch 8: speedup 1.381 vs 1.300 token on GPT Prompt.
limits: Gain is single-digit percent. Zero at temperature 0 (greedy), because it reduces to token verification. Gain grows with gamma and temperature, but wall clock peaks at gamma 4-6. Optimality is among valid verifiers in the standard outer loop only. Multi-draft extension left as future work.
use_for_project: Use as a lossless 5-8% wall-clock speedup, a free default for sampled decoding. Not a large cost lever. Because output distribution is identical, it carries no quality-risk term.
corrections: Earlier record said none, could not verify beyond abstract. Full text confirms the abstract and adds specifics: proofs of validity and optimality, no gain at temperature 0, wall-clock gain smaller than block-efficiency gain, and greedy block verification does worse empirically.
new_techniques: Greedy block verification (Appendix C): accepts more tokens per iteration but needs a distribution-modification step on later iterations. Empirically worse than block verification (BE 3.30 vs 3.49 on LM1B, token 3.21).
Block verification beats multi-draft SpecTr and SpecInfer on wall clock at batch 8 despite lower block efficiency (3.715 vs 3.898 SpecTr), because extra drafts cost compute.
Coupling view: block verification maximizes expected accepted prefix as an optimal-transport coupling between draft and target block distributions (Eq. 40).

algorithm: Supervised fine-tuning of facebook/opt-350m for 1 epoch (HF TRL SFTTrainer) on ToolBench converted to 187,542 Thought/Action/Action Input examples; LR 5e-5, effective batch 32, FP16, gradient checkpointing, 5,860 steps.
methodology: ToolBench/ToolEval, ChatGPT-judged pass rate, 6 categories, 1,100 test queries, temp 0.1, max 10 iterations, majority vote over at least 4 judge rounds. Baselines ChatGPT-CoT, ToolLLaMA-DFS/CoT, Claude-CoT.
key_numbers: Pass rate 77.55% overall vs ToolLLaMA-DFS 30.18%, ChatGPT-CoT 26.00%, ToolLLaMA-CoT 16.27%, Claude-CoT 2.73%; 74.0-80.5% across categories.
limits: Training data and evaluation tightly coupled; may not generalize beyond ToolBench; controlled API set; retraining needed as APIs evolve; still needs compute and data.
use_for_project: Row 12 (route tool-call steps to a small fine-tuned model). Weak evidence: benchmark-specific, no dollar or token cost measured.
corrections: Earlier record broadly right. Missed that the judge is ChatGPT, that no cost or token measurement exists despite the cost framing, and that the very low Claude-CoT baseline (2.73%) makes the comparison suspect.

algorithm: EmbedLLM: model-embedding network maps each model to a vector; question embedded with all-mpnet-base-v2 plus projection; linear classifier on the Hadamard product gives a correctness score (BCE loss). Router picks the model with highest predicted correctness; linear regression on embeddings predicts benchmark accuracy.
methodology: 112 open models, 36,054 questions from 10 benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, GPQA etc.), 80/10/10 question split. Compared with KNN, single-best and weighted-random routers.
key_numbers: Correctness forecasting 0.7409 (MF) vs 0.7152 (KNN) at 29K training questions. Routes 3,000 questions in 3.80 s on A100 (over 750/s, 15x the causal-LLM router). Training under 1GB GPU memory.
limits: Only 112 models so embeddings are sparse; new model needs retraining; correctness labels only; not agentic.
use_for_project: Row 12 router component. Needs per-model correctness logs from Token Economics's own traffic to train.
corrections: Earlier 'better routing accuracy and latency than prior methods' overstated: routing is compared only to single-best and weighted-random routers; the latency comparison is against one causal-LLM router (Ong et al.).
new_techniques: zero-shot benchmark accuracy prediction from model embeddings

algorithm: Qwen2.5-1.5B fully fine-tuned to generate a route-policy id given the conversation plus all policy (name, NL description) pairs in the prompt. A separate policy-to-model mapping is edited without retraining. Domain-Action taxonomy with fallback to domain if action is vague.
methodology: 43k synthetic samples built in two phases (clean data, then augmentation: irrelevance injection, policy modification, scenario mixing). Eval on CLINC-150, MANtIS, SGD, LMSYS-1M at turn, span and conversation level vs GPT-4o, Claude-sonnet-3.7, Gemini and others.
key_numbers: Overall 93.17 vs Claude-sonnet-3.7 92.79 and GPT-4o 89.74; turn 96.05, span 94.98, conversation 88.48. Authors cite +7.71% average over the compared models.
limits: Bounded by precision of policy descriptions; quality bounded by user's model-to-policy assignment; all policies sit in the prompt; no cost or answer-quality measurement.
use_for_project: Row 12 router component: policy-based routing where models can be swapped without retraining. Measures policy-match accuracy, not savings.
corrections: Earlier '+7.71% over top proprietary' is an average over all compared models; over the best (Claude-sonnet-3.7) it is +0.38. It is policy-match accuracy on synthetic dialogues, not cost savings.

algorithm: S1-S6 conversion recipe: log non-HCI agent calls; curate and filter (10k-100k examples, remove PII); cluster tasks; select SLM; fine-tune (LoRA/QLoRA/full, optional distillation); iterate and retrain SLMs and router.
methodology: Position paper with 13 arguments, barriers, an alternative view, and three case studies (MetaGPT, Open Operator, Cradle) with authors' estimates.
key_numbers: Cited from other work: 7B SLM 10-30x cheaper than 70-175B LLM. Authors estimate replaceable LLM queries: MetaGPT about 60%, Open Operator about 40%, Cradle about 70%.
limits: No measured savings; estimates are the authors'; acknowledges centralized LLM inference may still be cheaper per token (jury still out).
use_for_project: Row 12: instrumentation plan (log agent calls, cluster tasks) and a prior for what share of agent traffic could move to a small model.
corrections: Earlier 'no measured cost reduction' is right but missed the three 40-70% replaceable-query estimates and the explicit counter-arguments.
new_techniques: call-interface logging as SLM training data source

algorithm: Segment-wise gist compression: L tokens into t gist tokens (ratio L/t); compares memory location (recurrent vs KV) and granularity (coarse vs fine): Coarse-Rec, Coarse-KV, Fine-KV. Adds fine-grained autoencoding and segment-wise token importance estimation (TIE) to fix failures.
methodology: Llama3.1-8B and Qwen2-7B continued-trained on 3B SlimPajama tokens, ratios 4-32; eval on perplexity, weak-context and long-context tasks (RAG, rerank, QA, ICL, synthetic recall, summarization, code).
key_numbers: Fine-KV best, near-lossless on RAG, LongQA, summarization, ICL at low ratios; weak on rerank, synthetic recall and BBH. Autoencoding reconstruction under 20% at high ratios. At ratio 4 synthetic recall improved 52.7% and 33.7% by the two fixes.
limits: Models up to 7/8B, 16K window; only compared with full attention; requires continued training and KV access.
use_for_project: Row 17 (context compression): informs failure modes (exact recall, surprising facts, long reasoning chains). Not deployable through closed APIs.
corrections: Earlier record fine but missed BBH long-reasoning and rerank gaps, ratio dependence, and that all results need training and KV-level changes.

algorithm: No new method; diagnostic study. Each intermediate solution is re-executed to get a test-outcome vector; transitions labelled breakthrough/stay/improved/regressed/churn/broke/stuck; spans labelled with 12 behaviors by GPT-5-Mini; mixed-effects model on output tokens with problem as random effect.
methodology: mini-swe-agent, 5 models, 4 languages (Python, Java, Rust, OCaml), 100 LiveCodeBench v6 problems, 2,000 sessions, 40 turns, tests visible; metric is output tokens per trajectory (median).
key_numbers: OCaml uses 1.28-1.69x Python tokens (p<0.001). Gemma on OCaml: 1,196 stuck self-loops, 92% of failed snapshots are compile errors. Gemma/Qwen keep working after the first correct solution; over 70% of their spans into STAY are bare writes with no test run.
limits: One scaffold, competitive-programming problems only, 4 languages, 5 models; may not generalize to repo-scale work.
use_for_project: Rows 22 and 27 (post-success rework, compile-error loops): supports stop-after-all-tests-pass, repeated-identical-edit detection and compile-loop circuit breakers.
corrections: Earlier ranking right; missed the 1.28-1.69x size, post-solution waste, 92% compile-error loops, and 'wait/actually' second-guessing.
new_techniques: mixed-effects token model controlling problem difficulty

algorithm: LCPO: prompt adds 'Think for n_gold tokens' with n_gold ~ Uniform(100,4000); GRPO reward. L1-Exact: correctness minus 0.0003*|n_gold - n_y|. L1-Max: correctness times clipped length slack with delta 0.5, trained 120 steps after 700 of Exact.
methodology: DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview, 40K DeepScaleR data, 4K training context, 8K eval, targets 512-3600 tokens; AIME, MATH, AMC, Olympiad plus OOD GPQA, LSAT, MMLU.
key_numbers: Beats S1 by 20-25% absolute at 512/1024 tokens. L1-Max matches DeepScaleR-4K with up to 2x fewer tokens. Mean length error about 3% on math (20-40% OOD). Short CoT beats GPT-4o by about 2% at equal length.
limits: May not generalize to longer requested lengths; 4K training context; 1.5B math model (7B in appendix); little tuning.
use_for_project: Rows 29, 36, 45 (reasoning/thinking length): supports thinking-budget caps, but requires RL fine-tuning, so only analogous to API budget settings.
corrections: Earlier 'matches GPT-4o' is actually about +2% above GPT-4o on average; 'up to 20%' is 20-25% absolute. Missed L1-Max violation rate (0.3-2.3%) and that SFT on length-relabelled data fails.

algorithm: Sarathi-Serve: chunked prefills split a prompt into equal token-budget chunks; stall-free batching packs all running decodes first, then partial prefills, then new requests up to a token budget tau each iteration. Uniform hybrid batches also cut pipeline bubbles.
methodology: Built on vLLM; Mistral-7B (1 A100), Yi-34B (2 A100), LLaMA2-70B (8 A40), Falcon-180B (8 A100, TP4-PP2); openchat_sharegpt4 and arxiv_summarization traces; capacity under P99 TBT SLO.
key_numbers: Full-prefill hybrid batch raises TBT up to 28.3x vs decode-only. 3.5x vLLM capacity under strict 100ms SLO (Mistral-7B). Falcon-180B 4.3x and 3.6x over vLLM TP-only and hybrid, strict SLO.
limits: Chunking adds overhead for small chunks; token budget needs profiling; tile quantization (chunk 257 vs 256 adds 32% prefill time); no comparison with disaggregated systems.
use_for_project: none (provider-side scheduling; no client-controllable token leak).
corrections: Earlier record right but omitted that gains are capacity under latency SLOs, that the 2.6x/3.7x/5.6x are best cases, and the 28.3x stall evidence.

algorithm: Byte Latent Transformer: small byte-level entropy LM sets patch boundaries where next-byte entropy exceeds a threshold; lightweight local encoder pools bytes into patches via cross-attention, a large global transformer runs per patch, a local decoder emits bytes.
methodology: FLOP-controlled scaling study to 8B parameters and 4T bytes vs Llama 3 BPE; fixed-inference-FLOP study; robustness (noised HellaSwag, CUTE), FLORES-101 translation.
key_numbers: Matches Llama 3 at equal training FLOPs; patch size 8 allows nearly 50% fewer inference FLOPs with minor loss. BLT-Entropy beats Llama 3 on 4 of 7 tasks; CUTE gain over 25 points; noised HellaSwag +8 points.
limits: Scaling laws tuned for BPE; many experiments up to 1B; implementation not at wall-clock parity; separate entropy model.
use_for_project: none (model architecture; cannot be adopted via API).
corrections: Earlier '50% fewer flops' needs context: parity is at ~4.5-byte patches, the 50% figure is the ps=8 trade with a minor loss, and BLT-Space underperformed Llama 3 on all but one task.
new_techniques: entropy patching with approximate monotonicity constraint
byte-ifying a pre-trained Llama 3.1 global transformer

algorithm: HeadInfer: offloads KV cache to CPU per attention head, keeping only a few heads' KV on GPU while computing attention head by head; chunked prefill, asynchronous non-blocking PCIe transfer, adaptive head grouping; roofline analysis guides chunk size (10K).
methodology: Llama-3-8B and 70B, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma-2 on RTX-4090 24GB with 1TB CPU RAM; LongBench v2, SCBench, memory and throughput tests vs standard, chunked-prefill and layer-wise offload.
key_numbers: 1M-token Llama-3-8B: 207GB (15 weights, 64 activations, 128 KV) down to 17GB prefill / 16.4GB decode (92%). Max context 25K standard, 45K layer-wise, up to 4M with HeadInfer on one RTX-4090.
limits: Decode is memory-bound so PCIe slows it; short contexts suffer kernel-launch overhead; 70B prefill 7,210 tok/s but decode about 6 tok/s.
use_for_project: none (self-hosted memory optimization).
corrections: Earlier numbers correct but missing: lossless/exact attention, consumer-GPU target, and slow decode.
new_techniques: head-wise offload combined with head-wise sparsity

algorithm: Survey, no algorithm. Taxonomy of RACG by retrieval substrate, control regime and evaluation; agent autonomy levels L0 (static pipeline), L1 (iterative feedback), L2 (autonomous agents).
methodology: Literature review of repo-level retrieval-augmented code generation; RQs on methods, evaluation, and the necessity boundary between RAG and long context.
key_numbers: Agentless (L0) cited at 32% on SWE-bench Lite at low cost. Long-context models can match RAG on small repos (Peng et al. 2025).
limits: Survey only; no new measurements; cost and latency claims qualitative.
use_for_project: Rows 31 and 34 (retrieval vs reading whole repo): RepoShapley and OrcaLoca context pruning are named only in one-line summaries; the necessity-boundary section supports a size-based retrieval rule.
corrections: Shapley selection and OrcaLoca pruning are one-line mentions each; the survey gives no evidence of their savings.
new_techniques: agentic search replacing RAG (Claude Code grep/ls/cat loop)

algorithm: Elicit p(evidence|state) from M LLMs via contrastive 'assume state s' prompts, aggregate by median, apply Bayes with deployment prior, choose action by minimum expected cost, gather more evidence if value of information exceeds its cost or models disagree.
methodology: 1,000 synthetic resumes with sampled ground truth, GPT-4o-generated labels checked by 3 recruiters on 100 (kappa 0.83), simulated phone screens, 5 LLMs, hiring costs $40K/$2.5K/$150.
key_numbers: $294,000 (34%) lower total cost vs best single-LLM; parity gap 22 to 5 points. Ablation shares: multi-LLM 51%, sequential 43%, disagreement-triggered screening 20%. 20 LLM queries per observation (M=5, K=4).
limits: Synthetic data and simulated screens; latency of 20 queries per step; cost matrix assumed; model IDs and versions inconsistent between abstract and appendix.
use_for_project: Row 12 only weakly: savings are hiring dollars, not tokens; the ensemble multiplies calls 5x. Transferable idea: value-of-information gating of extra calls.
corrections: Earlier record omitted that the $294,000 is on synthetic resumes with simulated screens, is a hiring decision cost not LLM cost, and that the method uses 5 models x 4 states = 20 queries per observation.

algorithm: Inference auction: bids only reorder children in the SGLang radix-tree DFS schedule (keeps cache hit rate); children sorted by average subtree bid; VCG payments in quasilinear time; pacing autobidder scales values by a factor updated to hit a budget.
methodology: Scheduling layer over unmodified SGLang, 32B model on one H100, semi-synthetic stars, chains, 3-ary trees (SQuAD, GSM8K, SWE-agent trajectories, tree-of-thought), synthetic Pareto values, truthful bids.
key_numbers: Welfare +12-18.6% iid (up to 100% non-iid) over bid-blind cache-optimal order; about 80% of the unconstrained bid-sort welfare; bid-sort TTFT 2.4x on chains and 12x on long trees. Autobidding loses about 10% welfare.
limits: Single worker, simulated values, truthful bids, linear value in priority; short trees fit cache so DFS restriction costs 20% welfare.
use_for_project: none (provider-side mechanism; autobidder budget pacing is only an analogy for a per-task spend governor).
corrections: Earlier record right; missed that it is welfare, not dollars saved, with synthetic bids and O(sqrt T) regret guarantee only under a stationary assumption.
new_techniques: value-pacing autobidder with node pacing condition number

read: Full text of p.txt (1141 lines): abstract, sections 1 to 8, Table 1, Figures 1 to 11, Algorithm 1. Bibliography skimmed only to its start; remainder skipped. No appendices exist.
algorithm: Orca: iteration-level scheduling (scheduler invokes the engine for one model iteration at a time, so finished requests return and new ones join immediately) plus selective batching (batch non-Attention ops token-wise; split and run Attention per request). Algorithm 1 is FCFS with max_bs and K/V slot reservation.
methodology: 13K lines C++/CUDA on Azure ND96asr A100 40GB VMs, up to 4 VMs. GPT configs 13B, 101B, 175B, 341B, fp16, max sequence 2048. Baseline NVIDIA FasterTransformer with a custom scheduler. Synthetic Poisson trace: input U(32,512), max_gen_tokens U(1,128), EOS never emitted.
key_numbers: 175B model, median normalized latency 190 ms: FasterTransformer 0.185 req/s vs Orca 6.81 req/s, 36.9x. Engine microbenchmark: up to 47% faster at 175B, similar or slightly worse at 13B and 101B. FasterTransformer peak 0.49 req/s on 101B under load.
limits: Synthetic trace, no real workload. No EOS, so early stopping untested. Only GPT-style models measured. Max_bs needs tuning against a latency budget. K/V memory reserved at max_tokens, wasting slots. Tight scheduler-engine coupling; general interface left to future work.
use_for_project: None for API users directly. Provider-side serving technique; explains why continuous batching lowers provider cost per token, not a billing lever for callers.
corrections: Earlier record's 36.9x is correct but conditional: one 175B setting at matched 190 ms latency against a weak baseline, not a general figure. Add that the 101B model at low load showed no gain.
new_techniques: Iteration-level scheduling: one-iteration engine calls, immediate return and join
Selective batching: split only Attention, flatten token batches elsewhere
Max_tokens K/V slot reservation to avoid scheduler deadlock
Control-plane gRPC separate from NCCL data plane, up to 47% faster
Pipelining across batches without microbatch splitting

algorithm: Local proxy (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) with a rule-based O(1) router, no model calls. Requests with a non-empty tools field go straight to Opus. Simple prefixes go to the cheap model only (SKIPPED). Complex keywords or input over 1,500 chars get cheap draft then Opus verify (USE_DRAFT = ACCEPTED, or ENHANCE).
methodology: Service benchmark N=125 live Claude Code requests; 20-task engineering benchmark; 3-endpoint quality comparison (N=20 each, binary pass/fail). Baseline native Opus. Prices: DeepSeek $1.74/$3.48, Opus $5.50/$27.50 per M in/out.
key_numbers: Savings 45.8% (service, N=125), 47.4% (architecture set, N=39), 32% (current run, N=12); model predicted 67.2% vs 47.4% observed. p50 latency 2,026 vs 3,698 ms. Quality 100% vs 95% pass (N=20).
limits: Tool-selection turns (70-80% of Claude Code turns) bypass to Opus, so savings apply to the ~20-30% text turns. Router is a keyword classifier. One cost inversion (+$0.01189). TTFT 2.1x worse. Learned router, parallel draft+verify, local tier are future work.
use_for_project: Rows 12 and 5 (model tiering/routing); evidence for draft-then-verify cascade and the tool-turn carve-out.
corrections: Earlier record said tool-selection turns go to the cheap draft model; the opposite: they bypass to Opus and the draft handles only simple text turns. 45.8% applies only to the text-generation subset; the 100% vs 95% quality rests on a 20-task benchmark.
new_techniques: tool-call bypass to the strong model

algorithm: A base causal LM (LLaMA-7B; GPT-3 curie for OpenAI models) computes self-information -log2 P(x_t|x_<t) sentence by sentence. Tokens are merged into lexical units (tokens, noun phrases via spaCy, sentences). Units at or above the p-th percentile of self-information are kept.
methodology: BBC News, arXiv sections, ShareGPT (all after March 2023); tasks: reconstruction, summarisation, QA, conversation; GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA 7/13/30B, Vicuna. Ratios 0.2-0.8; BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore vs full context; random-deletion baseline; 1000 QA pairs hand-checked.
key_numbers: At ratio 0.5: BERTScore-F1 drop .023, unfaithfulness .038. At ratio 0.2: BERTScore-F1 .931 vs .899 random. Phrase-level units best. One vicuna-13b case: 36% memory (77,695 to 61,885 MB), 1.32x speed.
limits: Needs phrase-boundary detection (no verb phrases). Best percentile varies by task and context. Quality drops noticeably from ratio 0.5 up. Never tested on code or tool output.
use_for_project: Rows 17 and 37: context compression of prose-heavy context (documents, chat history), not code or tool output.
corrections: The 36% memory and 1.32x speed come from a single case-study paragraph, not an average. Quality figures are at ratio 0.5. The 'not code/tool output' caveat is untested by the authors rather than stated as a limit.
new_techniques: sentence-by-sentence self-information to avoid later-unit bias

algorithm: At paragraph breaks, probe a tentative answer by appending a final-answer prefix. Certainty C = 1 - mean token entropy / log|V|. Suppression probability p = max(0,(C-delta)/(1-delta)), delta=0.9. With probability p, trigger-token logits (Wait, But, Alternatively, Hmm and variants) are set very negative.
methodology: AIME24, AMC23, MATH500, GPQA-D. R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/Llama-8B, QwQ-32B, Qwen3-4/8/14/32B. vLLM, temp 0.6, three runs. Baselines: Vanilla, TALE, NoThinking, Dynasor, DEER.
key_numbers: 18.5-41.9% token reduction, accuracy drop up to about 3 points. Qwen3-14B: 25.4% fewer tokens, accuracy 80.1 to 80.8; NoThinking cuts 77.3% but loses 17.8% accuracy. AMC23 ablation: fixed p=1 gives 76.7 acc at 2373 tokens vs certainty-guided 88.3 at 3406 (vanilla 87.5 at 5861).
limits: Needs decoding-time logit access (open models). No overhead analysis found in the text read. Probing runs concurrently with decoding.
use_for_project: Row 45 (reasoning overthinking). Only the idea transfers to hosted APIs, via effort/thinking-budget controls.
corrections: 18.5-41.9% is a range across models, and accuracy loss is up to about 3 points, not zero. The hosted-API caveat is an inference, not stated by the authors.

algorithm: Six-step LLM-to-SLM conversion: secure logging of non-human-facing calls; curate and filter data (10k-100k examples rule of thumb, PII removal); task clustering; SLM selection; specialised fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA, optional distillation); iterate and retrain including the router.
methodology: Position paper, no experiments. Numbers are capability claims from other papers plus case-study estimates of replaceable query share: MetaGPT ~60%, Open Operator ~40%, Cradle ~70%.
key_numbers: 7B SLM 10-30x cheaper than 70-175B LLM in latency/energy/FLOPs (cited). Replaceable query share 40-70% across three agents (authors' estimates, not measured). SLM defined as under 10B params.
limits: Authors list opposing views: LLM generalists win on general language, centralisation economies of scale ('jury is still out'), equally possible worlds. Barriers: infrastructure investment, generalist benchmarks, awareness.
use_for_project: Rows 12 and 5: tiering and routing narrow, repetitive agent subtasks to small models.
corrections: Earlier 'no single cost number' is correct. Add the 40-70% replaceable-query estimates and that they are authors' estimates.
new_techniques: logger at the tool/model interface to harvest fine-tune data

read: Entire paper, main text sections 1-7 and appendices A-E, via pdftotext default and -layout. Read Appendix Table 1 (per-model accuracy and cost per dataset), hyperparameters, overalignment note and figure captions. Figure plot data read from AIQ legends only; Figure 3 heatmap and Figure 7 and 9 curves not readable as text. References skimmed.
algorithm: Routers are points in the cost-quality plane. Mixing two routers with probability t gives any point on their segment; extrapolation adds cost without quality. The non-decreasing convex hull is the Zero router; AIQ is hull area over [cmin, cmax] divided by the cost span. KNN and MLP routers pick argmax of lambda times predicted quality minus cost; the cascade calls models cheapest first until a judge passes.
methodology: 405,467 samples, 11 models plus 3 RAG-only (14 LLMs run), 8 datasets, 64 tasks: MMLU, MT-Bench, MBPP, HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-C, GSM8K and an 800-query RAG set. 5-shot on the exact-match sets, 0-shot on MBPP, MT-Bench, RAG graded by GPT-4. Predictive routers trained on 70%, tested on 30%, MT-Bench excluded (80 questions). Cascade judge is oracle-like with error flip probability.
key_numbers: Oracle: MMLU 0.957 at $0.297 vs GPT-4 0.828 at $4.086; HellaSwag 0.994 at $0.86 vs GPT-4 0.923 at $24.29. Predictive AIQ vs Zero: MMLU 0.773/0.769 vs 0.763; ARC 0.871/0.875 vs 0.877; MBPP 0.644/0.642 vs 0.660; HellaSwag 0.588 all. Cascade at zero error: MMLU 0.901, MBPP 0.862, ARC 0.923, GSM8K 0.680 (Zero 0.628), HellaSwag 0.469 vs Zero 0.607. RAG AIQ: KNN 0.695, MLP 0.675, cascade 0.657, Zero 0.632.
limits: Cost and quality only, no latency. Mostly academic multiple-choice tasks, 2023-era models, no coding agents or long contexts. Cost for predictive routers approximated by per-token price. Cascade judge is simulated with perfect knowledge, so results are an upper bound. Three tasks graded by GPT-4. RAG has few models and one client's queries. In-domain train and test split; out-domain test only plotted.
use_for_project: Row 12 and the evaluation framework: use AIQ with a Zero-router baseline (mix of existing models on the hull) to judge any Token Economics router, and require a router to beat Zero before claiming savings. Cascade results show the judge error rate is the lever.
corrections: Earlier record omitted that RAG is the eighth dataset and 3 of 14 LLMs are RAG-only. Its claim that cascades beat Zero at low judge error misses HellaSwag, where the zero-error cascade loses (0.469 vs 0.607). Exact AIQ values now given, including Zero beating both predictive routers on MBPP and ARC. GSM8K Zero AIQ is 0.632 in Fig 4 but 0.628 in Fig 5, an internal inconsistency.
new_techniques: AIQ: normalised area under the non-decreasing convex hull
Zero router baseline as probabilistic mix on the hull
Linear interpolation and extrapolation of routers with null router at zero cost
Oracle router: cheapest correct model, ties broken by price
Cascade with total-cost cap T and injected judge error epsilon
Predictive score lambda times predicted quality minus cost, lambda as willingness to pay
KNN (k=40, MiniLM, cosine) and 2x100 MLP quality predictors
Query features like 2024 route time-sensitive RAG queries to online models

algorithm: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: lightning indexer I=sum_j w_j ReLU(q_j.k_s) picks top-k=2048 KV entries per query, cutting core attention O(L^2) to O(Lk). Dense warm-up (1000 steps, KL loss) then sparse stage (15,000 steps). Agent: reasoning kept across tool-call turns, dropped only when a new user message arrives.
methodology: Benchmarks vs GPT-5-high, Kimi-K2-Thinking, Gemini-3.0-Pro; agent RL on 1,827 synthetic environments / 4,417 tasks; BrowseComp context-management comparison.
key_numbers: BrowseComp 51.4 without context management; Summary 60.2; Discard-all 67.6 (triggered at over 80% of context). Terminal Bench 2.0: 46.4 (Claude Code framework). Comparable to Kimi-K2-Thinking with substantially fewer output tokens.
limits: Token efficiency below Gemini-3.0-Pro; redundant self-verification pushes MCP tasks past 128K. Reasoning retention breaks in frameworks that simulate tool output as user messages (Roo Code, Terminus).
use_for_project: Rows on reasoning re-generation and context overflow: keep reasoning across tool rounds; summarise/discard at 80% context.
corrections: Earlier 'provider-side, no user lever, no rows' was shallow: it has agent context-management strategies and reasoning-retention finding that map to context and reasoning rows.

algorithm: Reuse precomputed per-chunk KV caches in non-prefix positions, then selectively recompute KV for high-KV-deviation tokens (HKVD). HKVD tokens are picked on the first layer and refined by progressively smaller ratios on later layers, since deviation rank is correlated across layers. Recompute is pipelined with loading KV from the next layer.
methodology: Built on vLLM; Mistral-7B, Yi-34B, Llama-70B on A40 GPUs with NVMe SSD; four datasets (2WikiMQA, Musique, MultiNews, SAMSum). Baselines: full recompute, prefix caching, full KV reuse, MapReduce, MapRerank.
key_numbers: TTFT 2.2-3.3x lower and throughput 2.8-5x higher than full recompute, at no quality loss. Default recompute ratio 15%; quality holds at 5-18%. Full KV reuse has similar TTFT but 0.1-0.2 lower F1.
limits: Transformer-only; self-hosted serving engine with KV storage. Not applicable to hosted APIs. Integration with newer serving engines left to future work.
use_for_project: none for user-side Token Economics; provider/self-host RAG prefill concern (adjacent to prefix-cache rows, no direct row).
corrections: Earlier '10-20% recompute' is approximately right (15% default, 5-18% range). Abstract and intro compare against different baselines (full recompute vs prefix caching), so state the baseline.
new_techniques: loading controller picking storage device and ratio

algorithm: PagedAttention: KV cache split into fixed-size blocks mapped by a block table, allocated on demand, not contiguous. Blocks are shared across sequences by reference count with copy-on-write (parallel sampling, beam search, shared prefix). On memory exhaustion, evict whole sequences and recover by swap or recompute.
methodology: vLLM on OPT and LLaMA models; ShareGPT and Alpaca traces; WMT16 for prefix sharing. Baselines: FasterTransformer and self-implemented Orca variants (Oracle, Pow2, Max).
key_numbers: 2-4x throughput over FasterTransformer/Orca at same latency. Existing systems use only 20.4-38.2% of KV memory for token states. 1.7-2.7x higher request rate than Orca (Oracle) on ShareGPT. Shared one-shot prefix: 1.67x over Orca (Oracle).
limits: Kernel overhead 20-26% higher attention latency vs FasterTransformer. Helps only memory-bound workloads; compute-bound DNNs may degrade.
use_for_project: none (provider-side memory management; no user lever).
corrections: none (2-4x confirmed; note Orca baselines are the authors' own reimplementation since Orca was not available)

algorithm: Train about 7,000 comparable monolingual tokenizers (BPE, Unigram) for 97 languages at 300MB, 7 vocab sizes (16,384-114,688). Measure corpus token count (CTC) on FLORES-200 parallel text. Interventions: parallel training data, per-language optimal vocab size via power-law fit, SuperBPE (merges across whitespace).
methodology: Linear mixed-effects models on CTC vs byte-premium scaling, tokenizer type, vocab size, word length, whitespace share, writing system. Compared with OLMo, Pythia, SmolLM tokenizers.
key_numbers: Token premiums vary widely even with identical training; raising vocab size does not shrink variance (F-test p=0.565). Per-language optimal vocab sizes significantly cut CTC variance (p<0.001). SuperBPE lowers mean CTC and variance at every vocab size.
limits: No link to downstream model performance tested. Small 300MB training data. Authors note too much compression may reduce compute per token.
use_for_project: Language-token premium (non-English prompts cost more tokens); no matching token-leak row unless one covers language. Advice: keep prompts/tool text in English.
corrections: Earlier record fine. Add: byte-premium scaling and parallel data had little effect; whitespace pre-tokenization is the main driver; a user cannot change a hosted tokenizer.
new_techniques: per-language optimal vocabulary size via power-law fit

algorithm: Two-model cascade (FLAN-T5 Base to Large). Deferral score from token-level uncertainty: Chow-Sum, Chow-Average, Chow-Quantile (quantiles of per-token probabilities), and a learned post-hoc MLP (5 layers, 32 units) on quantile features, optionally plus small-model and large-model intermediate embeddings.
methodology: 17 datasets (classification, QA, reading comprehension, translation, reasoning) up to 10k examples each; deferral curve and AUC-DF; 5 random runs; target = large right and small wrong (or BLEURT difference for translation).
key_numbers: Chow-Sum defers long outputs, Chow-Average defers short ones (length bias). Post-hoc rule is consistently best or near-best on AUC-DF. Using large-model first-token embedding helps most on classification.
limits: Only FLAN-T5 encoder-decoder; decoder-only and RLHF-calibration effects untested. Intermediate large-model embeddings add non-trivial cost. No single best quantile across tasks.
use_for_project: Row 12: confidence-based deferral for small-to-large cascades; needs token log-probs, which hosted APIs may not expose.
corrections: Earlier 'AUC-DF' fine. Missed length bias, no universal quantile, and that the best variant uses large-model embeddings (extra cost).

algorithm: Cost-Spectrum Contrastive Routing: prompts (frozen MiniLM + MLP head) and models embedded in one space. Models described by logit footprints (open models) or perplexity fingerprints (black-box APIs). Cost-Spectrum InfoNCE: banded positives (K=5), band-specific temperatures, cost-weighted negatives (gamma=0.2). Routing is one FAISS k-NN lookup.
methodology: EmbedLLM, Mix-Instruct, RouterBench. Metrics AUDC, peak accuracy, QNC. Baselines UMR, Thompson, others; unseen-LLM and OOD-prompt tests.
key_numbers: Best AUDC on all three benchmarks; up to 25% better accuracy-cost trade-off. OOD AUDC 0.5146 vs next-best 0.4863. Cost-aware loss lifts AUDC 0.342 to 0.495 and peak accuracy 36% to 54% (ablation).
limits: Did not test very large pools. Perplexity descriptor is at least 2x slower. Cost-aware training raises cost versus vanilla variant.
use_for_project: Row 12: learned prompt router; cheap lookup router if Token Economics has per-task outcome data.
corrections: 'Up to 25%' is a best case. Add: ablation gains, and that routing is trained on labelled correctness data.

read: pdftotext (default and -layout) of all 162 pages, read without line filtering. Read in full: sections 1-12, Appendices A through J, section 4.9 efficiency, Table 5 (tokens, queries, cost), Table 6 (hardware), Table 9 (GPT-3 energy), Table 13 (contamination), Table 14 (adaptation defaults). Skipped: bibliography only (pages 100-117). Figures were read as extracted text only, not visually. This PDF has no per-model results appendix; per-model data appear only in the tables listed above.
algorithm: HELM = scenarios x adaptation x metrics. 42 scenarios, 30 models, 16 families, 12 organizations. Adaptation is 5-shot in-context prompting with black-box access. Metrics: accuracy (exact match, quasi-exact match, F1, RR@10, NDCG@10, ROUGE-2, BPB, pass@k); calibration (ECE with uniform-mass bins, acc@10%, SCAA = (1/n) sum a_i); robustness (min over perturbations j of m(model(T_j(x_i)), y_i), identity transform included, so robustness is at most accuracy); fairness (same worst-case form on counterfactual perturbations, plus subgroup disparities compared by hand); bias (total variation distance of group mentions or stereotype associations from a uniform reference; maximum 0.5 for gender, 2/3 for race); toxicity (fraction of generations with Perspective API score >= 0.5); efficiency (training energy e = n_GPU * W_GPU * t_train * PUE with PUE 1.1, CO2 = energy times carbon intensity; inference denoised and idealized runtime).
methodology: Adaptation: 5 fixed in-context examples chosen by class coverage, 3 seeds, 1000 evaluation instances per scenario. Temperature 0 for short outputs; stop sequence newline, with max tokens set from the longest reference as a fail-safe; prompts truncated to the context window. Multiple choice is joint by default (one query per question), separate for natural continuations. Ranking uses per-passage Yes/No queries over BM25 top-30 passages. Robustness recipe: lowercase, expand contractions, misspell each word with probability 0.1, replace each space with 1 to 3 spaces; also contrast sets for BoolQ and IMDB. Fairness perturbations: SAE to AAE dialect, gender pronouns, gender terms, first names, last names; references perturbed the same way; perturbations deterministic. Robustness and fairness apply only to classification, QA and retrieval scenarios. Denoised runtime = provider hardware with queue noise removed; idealized runtime = A100 GPUs with Megatron, only for models with public architecture. Total time = F(num_prompt_tokens) + g * num_output_tokens. Run priorities 1 to 4; all models run on priority 1 and 2. Significance tests: paired bootstrap, 10,000 samples, p < 0.05. Disinformation human evaluation on 6 models.
key_numbers: 4,939 runs, 12,169,227,491 tokens, 17,431,479 queries, $38,001 for commercial APIs (Cohere's $1,743 is one combined total across its four rows), about 19,500 GPU hours for open models. Per-model cost $85 (code-cushman-001) to $10,926 (J1-Jumbo v1). 98 of 112 (scenario, metric) pairs measured (87.5%). Seed range: median below 0.03 for 24 of 28 models; NaturalQuestions open-book median range 0.1730 (davinci F1 0.376, 0.611, 0.636). text-davinci-002 wins accuracy comparisons over 90% of the time. Win rate clearly above chance (above 55%) only for models of at least 50B parameters. text-davinci-002 HellaSwag accuracy 81.5%, TruthfulQA accuracy 62.0% against 35.4% for second place (Anthropic-LM v4-s3); those are accuracy figures, not fairness. Its fairness-perturbed HellaSwag accuracy is 70.3%; Cohere xlarge drops more than 15 points to 66%. OPT (175B) HellaSwag: 79.1% separate 0-shot, 54.8% separate-calibrated, 30.2% joint 5-shot. Denoised inference time BLOOM 0.075s separate vs 0.271s joint; text-davinci-002 idealized denoised ranking request 0.21s per query-passage pair. Training CO2: GPT-J 13.8 metric tons, TNLG v2 405.3 metric tons.
limits: Authors' caveats: 3 seeds and 1000 instances may leave some claims insignificant; contamination unresolved (Table 13, Pile-trained models flagged); prompting only, no fine-tuning; dataset validity unverified; no single aggregate score; missing scenarios, metrics, models (Gopher, PaLM) and adaptation methods. Robustness and fairness cover only classification, QA and retrieval, with mild synthetic perturbations; fairness by perturbation is a weak proxy for dialects. Idealized runtime exists only for models with public architecture, and idealized energy and CO2 cannot be derived from denoised runtime. Training energy mostly estimated. Disinformation judged by crowd workers on 6 models. Cost figures are API spend at 2022 prices, not a price model.
use_for_project: Not a cost-control method. Use as a measurement template: report accuracy beside cost and tokens for every run (Table 5 gives tokens, queries, $ per model); use worst-case-over-perturbations for a robustness check on routed or cached answers; report seed ranges; the F(prompt) + g * output runtime model matches the prompt-versus-output token split that drives dollar cost. Efficiency in HELM is runtime and energy, not dollars per task. Joint versus separate multiple choice shows prompt format changes both accuracy and query count, so cost comparisons must fix adaptation.
corrections: Earlier record confirmed on 3 seeds, 1000 instances, denoised and idealized runtimes. text-davinci-002 correction kept: 81.5% HellaSwag accuracy and 62.0% TruthfulQA accuracy are accuracy, not fairness; its fairness-perturbed HellaSwag score is 70.3%. Corrected: the 79.1% OPT figure is for separate 0-shot prompts (joint 5-shot is 30.2%); total commercial cost $38,001 counts Cohere's $1,743 once. Added: exact token and query totals, perturbation recipe, 5-shot class-coverage sampling, human evaluation limited to 6 models. Read now covers every page except the bibliography.
new_techniques: Metric inclusion rule: measure a desideratum only if it needs no knowledge of model construction, only black-box access, and no knowledge of the broader system.
Denoised runtime (provider stack, queue noise removed) versus idealized runtime (uniform A100 with Megatron); idealized energy and CO2 derivable only from the latter.
Runtime model: total time = F(num_prompt_tokens) + g * num_output_tokens.
Selective classification at coverage 0.1 and area under the coverage-accuracy curve (SCAA), reported beside ECE.
Fixed in-context examples across instances, chosen for class coverage, repeated over 3 seeds to expose prompt sensitivity.
Worst-case accuracy across a perturbation set with identity included, as one robustness number, reused for fairness with counterfactual substitutions.
Bias as total variation distance from a uniform reference; association bias counted only where the target term appears.
Joint versus separate multiple-choice ablation: OPT HellaSwag 79.1% separate 0-shot vs 30.2% joint 5-shot; separate needs one query per choice.
Run priorities 1 to 4 with a knapsack-style budget selection of scenario-model runs.
Contamination register (model x scenario, evidence) published as Table 13; coverage matrix of prior evaluations (42 x 30).
Per-scenario Pearson correlation between metric pairs to show when trade-offs are scenario-dependent.

algorithm: Budget forcing: cap thinking by appending the end-of-thinking delimiter (optionally 'Final Answer:'), or lengthen it by suppressing that delimiter and appending 'Wait'. Applied to Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct fine-tuned on s1K (1,000 curated questions from a 59K pool).
methodology: s1K chosen by quality, difficulty, diversity filters. Trained 26 minutes on 16 H100 (7 H100 hours). Evaluated AIME24, MATH500, GPQA Diamond; compared token/step/class-conditional control and rejection sampling; majority voting, REBASE.
key_numbers: AIME24 50.0 to 56.7 with budget forcing; MATH500 93.0; beats o1-preview by up to 27% (MATH, AIME24). 59K-full training costs 394 H100 hours vs 7 for s1K with no substantial gain.
limits: Scaling flattens after about six forced Waits and can loop. Context window caps scaling. Token-conditional control fails (model cannot count tokens); rejection sampling shows inverse scaling.
use_for_project: Row 45 (reasoning length control): hard cap on thinking is controllable; forced extension is the opposite of a saving. Only transfers via API thinking-budget settings.
corrections: The 50 to 57 and 27% hold. Add: 'up to 27%' is vs o1-preview on MATH/AIME24 and gains flatten; budget forcing targets more compute, so it is not a cost saver by itself.

read: Read directly, whole of dl/A033/p.txt, lines 1-1182 in two chunks: body, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-6, figures as extracted text only, Appendices A-B. Nothing skipped.
algorithm: Agent Forest: sample N outputs from the same LLM, then majority-vote. Code tasks vote by BLEU similarity between samples; closed-ended tasks by answer frequency. Combinable with CoT, debate and other prompting. Hierarchical variant votes within sub-groups, then across groups.
methodology: Single versus ensemble sizes up to 40 on Llama2-13B/70B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 across GSM8K, MATH, Chess, MMLU, HumanEval. Studies gain against steps, sub-task share and prior probability 1/K, with ANOVA at p<0.05 for all sizes.
key_numbers: Gains: GSM8K 12-24%, MATH 6-10%, Chess 1-4%, MMLU 5-11%, HumanEval 4-9%. Llama2-13B GSM8K .35 to .59; GPT-3.5 .73 to .85. Hierarchical: 21% to 31% homogeneous, 35% to 47% GPT-3.5+GPT-4. Table 5 single-run tokens 138-495.
limits: Cost scales with N: every sample is a full generation. Curves stop at N=40. Gain peaks at mid inherent difficulty (steps 100-200) then tapers at 400. Debate on Llama2 HumanEval gave 0 to 0. Code voting relies on BLEU.
use_for_project: Use as an N-fold token multiplier for an accuracy gain. Table 4: Agent Forest has the best average rank, 2.5. Do not cite a saturation point, because the paper gives none.
corrections: Earlier record repeated a commenter's asymptote near 30 agents. Text shows curves only to N=40 and no such claim. Also adds the non-monotonic difficulty finding, Tables 5-6 and the hierarchical variant.
new_techniques: BLEU-similarity voting: pick the sample with highest summed BLEU to the others, so voting works for code.
Hierarchical Agent Forest: vote inside groups, then across group winners; lets a cheap model and GPT-4 be mixed.
Difficulty properties: gain rises with number of steps and with prior probability 1/K, and is non-monotonic in inherent difficulty.
Orthogonal stacking: ensembling adds on top of CoT, debate and other prompting methods.

algorithm: SLM-default routing: small model with guided decoding and validators handles the task; uncertainty or validation failure escalates to a large model. Track Cost per Successful task (CPS) and schema validity; rollback thresholds trigger fallback.
methodology: Position/survey-style paper; Table II holds placeholder illustrative data, not measurements.
key_numbers: Body claims 10-30x lower cost; abstract says 10x-100x (inconsistent).
Table II is placeholder data.
limits: Not a controlled experiment; headline factors unmeasured.
use_for_project: Row 12 (route to cheaper model) and row 27; adopt CPS as a metric and validator-gated escalation as a design pattern.
corrections: Prev says 10x-100x; body says 10-30x and the supporting table is placeholder. Overstated as an effect.

algorithm: Extends the MoE scaling law with inference cost per token as a constraint; compares loss-optimal MoEs with over-trained smaller-expert MoEs that trade extra training tokens for cheaper serving.
methodology: Scaling-law fits across MoE configurations (expert counts) with training-token and inference-cost accounting.
key_numbers: Same quality at 47.0-52.0% of inference cost vs loss-optimal 4-expert MoE.
Training budget 68.4% in one setting.
2.4-4.3x (intro) vs 2.5-3.5x (abstract) more training cost for 4/8-expert MoEs.
23.7-42.8% FLOPs reduction.
limits: Model-provider training concern; does not apply to API users or agent sessions.
use_for_project: none
corrections: Prev quotes 2.5-3.5x; intro states 2.4-4.3x. Adds the 23.7-42.8% FLOPs figure.

algorithm: Workload-binned energy model: bin input/output token lengths and batch sizes, measure energy under batching, decoding strategy and parallelism, compare to theoretical bounds.
methodology: Measured energy of serving stacks (vLLM, speculative decoding, tensor parallel, MoE) across workload bins.
key_numbers: Up to 73.00% energy saving vs unoptimized baseline (also 37.58%, 72.18% in other settings).
vLLM within 26.59-64.22% of theoretical.
Speculative decoding saves 29.14% at batch<=16 but costs 25.65% more energy at batch 128.
limits: Energy not dollars; provider-side.
use_for_project: none
corrections: Prev gives only the 73% best case; misses that speculative decoding raises energy at large batch (+25.65% at batch 128).

algorithm: RouterDC: encoder plus learnable LLM embeddings, trained with sample-LLM and sample-sample contrastive losses; route a query to the LLM whose embedding is most similar. Clustering similar queries stabilises training.
methodology: Candidate-LLM scores on training queries supply labels; evaluated in-distribution and out-of-distribution.
key_numbers: Average 58.54 vs 54.56 (+3.98) in-distribution; OOD 45.85 vs 43.95 (+1.90).
About 6x faster than voting.
limits: Needs scored training data per candidate LLM. Limitations section only says scenarios are left to future work.
use_for_project: Row 12: learned model routing; needs training data, so treat as optional.
corrections: Abstract reports +2.76 in-distribution but body shows +3.98 (comparator not determined); prev mixes the two. Adds the ~6x speed over voting.

algorithm: THINK-Bench: 1375 questions; metrics for thinking efficiency, useful tokens and reflection quality over reasoning-model chains.
methodology: Evaluation of reasoning models on a curated question set; no mitigation tested.
key_numbers: 1375 questions.
Efficiency Grok-3-mini 61.69% vs QwQ-plus 44.58%.
limits: Benchmark only; no mitigation.
use_for_project: Rows 45 and 29 (overthinking): evidence for measuring wasted reasoning tokens.
corrections: Prev vague on numbers; adds efficiency values above.

algorithm: AWQ: weight-only PTQ (W4A16, INT3/INT4, group 128), no backprop. Salient channels chosen by activation magnitude; per-channel scale s=s_X^alpha, Q(w*s)(x/s); alpha by grid search (20 points) minimizing layer output error; plus weight clipping. TinyChat adds fused dequantization and SIMD-aware packing.
methodology: Calibration on a small Pile sample; WikiText-2 perplexity; GPT-4 judging on Vicuna (160 trials); models LLaMA, Llama-2, OPT, Mistral, Mixtral, Vicuna, VILA, OpenFlamingo, CodeLlama.
key_numbers: Llama-2-7B INT3-g128 PPL: AWQ 6.24 vs RTN 6.66 vs GPTQ 6.43 (FP16 5.47).
16 calibration sequences suffice vs 192 for GPTQ; distribution shift raises PPL 0.5-0.6 vs 2.3-4.9 for GPTQ.
TinyChat 2.7-3.9x over HF FP16 on RTX 4090; Llama-2-13B 33 tok/s on laptop 4070.
OpenFlamingo-9B COCO INT4 drop: AWQ -1.17, RTN -4.57, GPTQ -6.72.
limits: Weight-only: no help for compute-bound large-batch prefill; focus is batch size 1 on-device; perplexity is the main metric.
use_for_project: Self-hosted serving cost lever (quantization); no direct token-leak row.
corrections: Prev says more than 3x speedup; body gives 2.7-3.9x desktop and up to 1.7x vs llama.cpp. Adds calibration robustness and AWQ+GPTQ INT2 combination.

algorithm: TokenLake: segment-level prefix cache pool with declarative interface (get_prefix_tree, get_cache_load, gen_plans; init_query, query, init_transfer, put). Heavy-hitter-aware load balancing (hash normal segments, replicate top heavy hitters), power-of-two-choices replica pick, global LRU, bipartite-matching dispatch, DP goodput scheduler.
methodology: 16k-LOC prototype on FlashInfer/SGLang/LoongServe; 8xA100-80GB, Llama-2-7B based LWM-1M; LooGLE, SCBench, ShareGPT; baselines SGLang-Router and MoonCake.
key_numbers: Throughput up to 2.6x vs cache-aware routing, 2.0x vs PD disaggregation.
P90 goodput 2.55x on SCBench vs SGLang-Router.
Load-balance CV 11% vs 99% (Router) and 62%/122% (MoonCake).
Segment size threshold about 568 tokens.
limits: GPU-cluster infrastructure needing high-bandwidth interconnect; tested on 7B; gains concentrate in long-context multi-turn.
use_for_project: Prefix-cache hit-rate lever for self-hosted serving; not applicable to API-only use. Cites 75-95% production hit rates and Manus 100:1 input:output ratio as context.
corrections: Prev says none relevant; relevant only to the cache-hit-rate lever when self-hosting. Adds concrete numbers.

algorithm: Router is a 3B LLM policy trained with PPO that interleaves think with search calls to a pool of 6 LLMs (max 4 routing steps). Reward = format + (1-alpha)*EM outcome + alpha*cost; hierarchical (format failure zeroes others); cost normalized with sliding-window percentiles. New LLMs added via descriptors without retraining.
methodology: Trained on 14K NQ+HotpotQA samples; 7 QA datasets, 500 test each, Exact Match; Together API pricing for cost.
key_numbers: Average EM 0.416 (Qwen router) and 0.409 (Llama router) above baselines.
Adding two unseen LLMs: average EM 0.458 to 0.463 without retraining.
Average API calls about 1.01-1.36.
Alpha 0.6-0.9: performance falls as cost reward rises; emergent small-first then escalate.
limits: QA only with Exact Match; cost reward studied only for QA; router itself costs 3B inference per step; no cost-weighted Pareto in the main table.
use_for_project: Row 12 / model-routing component: cost-aware learned router; needs RL training, QA-only evidence.
corrections: Prev found no cost figure; body gives EM numbers and alpha trade-off but still no dollar saving.

algorithm: LiveBench: 18 tasks in 6 categories built from recent sources (arXiv, news, Kaggle, competitions), scored automatically against ground truth with no LLM judge; about 1/6 of questions replaced each monthly update.
methodology: 40 LLMs (0.5B to 405B), single-turn, temperature 0, zero-shot CoT, scores 0-1 averaged per task, category, overall.
key_numbers: Top model o1-preview 64.7; claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 58.5; all below 70%.
Correlation with Chatbot Arena 0.91 and Arena-Hard 0.88.
Rank correlation between updates > 0.997; mean score drops about 1.2% as questions refresh.
limits: No non-English tasks; ground truth cannot cover open-ended tasks; prompt-style biases across model families.
use_for_project: none directly; usable as a contamination-limited quality check when validating cheaper-model substitutions.
corrections: Prev none; body also gives Appendix B token/cost per API model (not read).

algorithm: Budget Tracker: plug-in that shows remaining and used per-tool budgets each ReAct iteration. BATS: structured tree plan (exploration vs verification clues), self-verification with SUCCESS/CONTINUE/PIVOT decisions, trajectory summarization, LLM judge picks final answer. Unified cost = token cost (input/output/cache) + tool-call cost.
methodology: Web search agents (search, browse) on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, HLE-Search, plus tau2-bench retail; Gemini-2.5-Pro; budget 100 per tool.
key_numbers: Budget Tracker at budget 10 matches ReAct at 100 (12.8% vs 12.6%) with 40.4% fewer search calls, 19.9% fewer browse calls, 31.3% lower cost.
BATS 24.6% BrowseComp, 46.0% BrowseComp-ZH, 27.0% HLE-Search, training-free.
Ablation: removing verification drops BrowseComp 18.7% to 15.4%.
limits: Evaluated on web search agents only; tool-call budget, not token budget.
use_for_project: Rows 27 and 5: expose remaining budget to the agent to curb runaway tool calls.
corrections: Prev omits the 40.4% fewer search calls and that the saving is at budget 10 vs 100; also BATS accuracy numbers.

algorithm: RetroInfer: wave index (cluster-based vector index over KV: GPU-resident centroids meta index) with tripartite attention approximation (steady, retrieval, estimation zones), accuracy-bounded estimation from centroids, segmented clustering; wave buffer with CPU-managed GPU block cache.
methodology: Llama3.1-8B, Llama3-8B-1048K, Qwen2.5-7B/72B and R1-distill models on A100; RULER and long-context tasks; baselines Quest, MagicPIG, InfiniGen, PQCache.
key_numbers: Up to 4.4x decoding throughput over full attention at 120K, up to 12.2x over sparse baselines.
Accuracy +1.40-46.47% over sparse baselines at same retrieval budget.
Attention estimation improves accuracy up to 20%.
limits: Inference-engine internals needing GPU/CPU control; not usable by API users.
use_for_project: none; self-hosted long-context serving only.
corrections: Prev is accurate; adds accuracy gains and ablation.

algorithm: Empirical study: GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, FP8 applied to Llama 1B-405B instruction models; 13 datasets in 6 categories plus MT-Bench with GPT-4 judge.
methodology: Multi-cluster GPU evaluation; OpenLLM Leaderboard v1/v2 tasks and MT-Bench.
key_numbers: Llama-3.2-1B 4-bit: -25.32% GSM8K, -16.01% IFEval.
Llama-3.1-8B: 8-bit beats 4-bit by +2.51%/+2.11%; at 70B 4-bit beats 8-bit by +1.89%.
FP8 most stable; SmoothQuant poor on 405B; AWQ usually beats GPTQ.
limits: Runtime limits (over 30 days) prevented some configs; GPT-4 judge errors; no cost measurements.
use_for_project: Self-hosting quantization choice; no token-leak row.
corrections: Prev accurate; adds task difficulty finding (little effect), MT-Bench coding/STEM drops, FP8 halves KV cache.

algorithm: Mechanism design: buyers have type (willingness-to-pay, task volume, time preference); hardware tiers induce self-selection on time preference (separation theorem), reducing to 1-D Mussa-Rosen screening per tier; per-task prices independent of volume.
methodology: Cost model from prefill/decode physics, latency quadratic in input; calibrated to 8-GPU H100 and B200 clusters; 105 configurations.
key_numbers: Separation theorem holds in 83% of 105 configurations, 96% at relevant WTP scales.
Two-tier gives 26-66% higher seller profit than best single tier.
No quantity discounts, matching flat per-token pricing.
limits: Monopolist, independence assumptions; no queueing; one hardware pair with decode ratio 0.68.
use_for_project: none; seller-side theory, useful only to reason about priority/fast-mode price tiers.
corrections: Prev accurate; adds assumptions and that gains are regime-dependent (single tier suffices for generational upgrades).
